summary:
Antigua and Barbuda requires real caution. In July 2022 the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court struck down Sections 12 and 15 of the Sexual Offences Act 1995, decriminalising sodomy and gross indecency between adults, and read the constitutional prohibition on sex discrimination to cover sexual orientation and gender identity as well.

That ruling does not amount to a statutory protection regime. No explicit anti-discrimination protection on the grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity exists in Antiguan and Barbudan law, and same-sex unions are not recognised. A visitor who is refused service, housing or transport on these grounds has no statute to invoke, only the constitutional argument the court opened in 2022.

There is no mechanism to change a legal gender marker. Only name changes are available, and Outright International records that transgender people are particularly vulnerable in Antigua and Barbuda precisely because no legal gender recognition process exists. A visitor whose passport marker does not match their presentation should expect that mismatch to be visible at every point where documents are checked.

Social hostility remains a live factor. Orden David, the Antiguan activist who brought the challenge that produced the 2022 judgment, was bullied and physically attacked before his case succeeded, including being struck in the head and knocked out in daylight. Tourist resort areas are comparatively insulated, but that insulation is a matter of circumstance rather than legal protection.

The protection machinery is unfinished. A January 2025 submission from The Advocates for Human Rights to the UN Human Rights Committee, filed ahead of its review of Antigua and Barbuda, sets out the SOGI-protection questions the state still faces after decriminalisation, indicating that the post-2022 legal position remains under international scrutiny rather than settled.
tangentialFactors:
Antigua and Barbuda sits inside a wider regional pattern rather than standing apart from it. Six Caribbean countries still criminalise same-sex conduct, and the 2022 judgment came out of a coordinated legal strategy: in December 2019 the Eastern Caribbean Alliance for Diversity and Equality (ECADE) announced court challenges to buggery and indecency laws in Barbados, St Kitts-Nevis, Antigua and Barbuda, Grenada and Saint Lucia, arguing that those laws stigmatise and legitimise hate speech, discrimination and violence against LGBT people.

The direction of travel across the Eastern Caribbean is therefore toward decriminalisation, but the pace is uneven and the accompanying protections have not followed the penalties out of the statute book. Comparable states that retain the offences provide a reference point for what a reversal would look like, and litigation of this kind remains subject to appeal and to legislative change.
localsOnly:
Residents can change a name but cannot change a legal gender marker, so the identity documents a resident carries will continue to show the sex assigned at birth indefinitely. There is no process, administrative or judicial, that produces a corrected marker.

Same-sex unions are not recognised, which affects inheritance, hospital visitation, next-of-kin decisions and immigration sponsorship for Antiguan and Barbudan couples. No anti-discrimination statute covers sexual orientation or gender identity in employment, housing, education or public accommodation, so residents must rely on the constitutional reading established in the 2022 judgment, case by case.

Orden David's litigation is the origin of the current constitutional position, and his experience of bullying and physical assault before the ruling reflects the environment local LGBT people navigated in the absence of legal protection. The pending review by the UN Human Rights Committee, with the January 2025 Advocates for Human Rights submission on the record, keeps the outstanding SOGI-protection questions formally before an international body.
outOfScopeNotes:
The consequence axis of an arrest is undocumented. The Outright International country profile (page states 'Last Update: March 12, 2026') contains no data on trans-prisoner housing placement: no birth-sex versus identity rule, no trans-specific units, no solitary or segregation practice. In a jurisdiction with no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination statute, a detained trans visitor would enter a prison system whose treatment of them is not described in any source held here.

Entry and visa screening are not covered by this inventory. Whether immigration or security screening asks about gender marker, sex or transition status, and what happens on a mismatch between a passport marker and presentation at the border, is unresolved and not sourced.

Facility access rules, including restroom and changing-room use in hotels, airports and public buildings, are not sourced. Nor is access to gender-affirming healthcare, its availability locally, or whether a visitor could obtain it.

It is also unresolved whether the 2022 constitutional reading of 'sex' has been applied in any decided case since the judgment, or how a court would handle a discrimination claim brought by a transgender complainant specifically rather than a sexual-orientation claim.
